title: LoRA vs full fine-tuning
paper: Hu et al. 2021, LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
claim: Training only low-rank adapters (a tiny fraction of the weights) matches full fine-tuning quality, and very low ranks are already enough.
setup: prajjwal1/bert-tiny on a 4000-sentence SST-2 subset, evaluated on 872 validation sentences. 3 epochs, 5 seeds. LoRA on query/value, ranks [1, 4, 16]; learning rates 0.0001 (full) and 0.001 (LoRA), not tuned beyond that.
result: Full FT accuracy 0.767 ± 0.017 with 100% trainable parameters. lora_r1 0.726 ± 0.015 (0.03% trainable); lora_r4 0.733 ± 0.027 (0.10% trainable); lora_r16 0.728 ± 0.020 (0.38% trainable). Best LoRA (lora_r4) is 3.3 accuracy points below full FT (seed std up to 2.7 points). Training took 61s (full) vs 37s (LoRA r=4), 1.6x faster; analytic training-state memory 66.9 MB vs 16.8 MB.
verdict_reason: LoRA gets within 3.3 points of full FT using under 0.4% of the parameters, but the gap is larger than the seed-to-seed spread, so parity is not shown at this scale.
mismatches: The paper reports parity with full FT on large models; here a gap remains on a 4.4M-parameter model.
Accuracy does not increase with rank (r=1, 4, 16 are within noise of each other), which agrees with the paper's 'low rank suffices' point but means we cannot show a rank trend.
Memory is an analytic estimate (weights + gradients + Adam states), not measured peak memory; activations are excluded.
Learning rates were set once, not swept; the LoRA/full gap may shrink with tuning.
